 Refund, anyone? Question 5 campaigns try to stay out of the weeds as voters (and lawmakers) make up their minds 
 Top lawmakers expected an income tax cut to pass, but the surviving ballot measure's fate is less clear. 
 Katie Lannan / 
 Oct 28, 2026

 On a clear October afternoon, with the sun bouncing off yellow and orange leaves, the Raise Up Massachusetts coalition posted a "Rainy Day Advisory" to Instagram.  
 The coalition's post cautions of a "higher risk of major budget cuts during economic downturns," warning of the potential for cuts at public colleges, MassHealth and job training programs during recessions.  
 A few days earlier, the Taxpayers for an Affordable Massachusetts committee posted an image on Facebook of cartoon coins sliding into the outline of a pocket. The caption makes a comparison: "When you hand a cashier $20 for a $17 charge, you expect to get $3 back in change. Why should government collections work any differently?" 
 The last time taxes were on the ballot, in 2022, the campaigns for and against the millionaire's tax question spent a staggering $43.5 million on efforts to persuade voters.  
 Beacon Hill had been bracing for another blockbuster ballot battle among unions, business groups, lawmakers and other interested parties. Instead, the Supreme Judicial Court tossed this year’s marquee tax question off the ballot, turning what had been the tax-relief undercard into the main event. 
 The disqualified question was simple (though opponents argued its consequences would be severe), asking voters if they’d like to cut their income tax rate from 5% to 4%. It polled high, and top lawmakers expected it to pass, eventually slicing billions of dollars out of state revenue collections, because, as House Speaker Ron Mariano once put it, “there aren't many people out there that're going to go to the polls and ... not vote to give themselves a tax cut.”  
 Days out from Election Day, the prospects of the surviving measure aren’t quite as clear-cut.  
 Designed to revise a rarely triggered law and generate more frequent rebates for taxpayers, Question 5 presents voters with the much wonkier choice of if they want to “change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit.” 
 It’s no wonder the campaigns are opting for social media-friendly metaphors instead of pulling the words directly from the ballot. They’re also spending at a relatively subdued rate so far compared to some of the other ballot questions — with a total of $1.24 million expended for and against, Question 5 ranks as the sixth spendiest of the nine ballot questions at this point.  
 By and large, the arguments are almost the same as they were for the income tax cut — on the one hand, that residents navigating an affordability crisis deserve direct relief while state spending climbs, and on the other, that diverting money from the state’s coffers would constrain public programs that offer broader benefits than the savings for any individual household.  
 A recent Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll suggests voters are still working through it, with 40% saying they'd vote yes, 38% no, and 20% undecided.  
 Also undecided: whether the Legislature will ultimately complicate the refunds issue further (and if they’ll do so in the next six days). A Senate -approved measure tied up in economic development bill talks would also add new limits on when the tax refunds get triggered.  
 What’s your take on Question 5 and how it will fare? Send me your thoughts at [email protected] .

 ON BEACON HILL 
 SHERIFFS SAY: A bipartisan group of 12 sheriffs wrote to Gov. Healey , flagging what they call an unintended consequence of the PROTECT Act she signed this summer to limit federal immigration enforcement activities in Massachusetts, and her challenger Mike Minogue highlighted their concerns in a Beacon Hill press conference. Meanwhile, the state's 12 Democratic sheriffs (including 10 who signed the letter) endorsed Healey's reelection bid, and the governor says she'll keep talking with sheriffs about the law. | State House News Service (gift link) 
 MAIL CALL: Secretary of State Bill Galvin says any voters who have yet to send their mail-in ballots should instead hand-deliver them to drop boxes or local election offices this close to Election Day. | Gloucester Times 
 CAUGHT OFF BASE: A pair of lawsuits, set for a hearing today in Suffolk Superior Court , seek a third year of rental assistance through the HomeBASE program for families struggling to pay for housing. The state's housing office says it paused approvals for a third year of aid to help as many families as possible with available resources. | GBH News 
 WHAT'S NEXT: Election Day won't necessarily be the end of the road for some ballot fights, with lawmakers able to change voter-approved laws like they did with a rewrite of the 2016 marijuana legalization question. | WBUR

 ORDER UP: Boston Mayor Wu laid out proposals aimed at making it quicker, easier and less expensive to open restaurants in the city, while also announcing former Cannabis Control Commission member Ava Callender Concepcion as the new executive director of her office of Consumer Affairs and Licensing and chair of the Boston Licensing Board. | Boston Herald 
 COUNTY DOWN: A non-binding ballot question in Braintree, Foxboro and Norfolk asks voters if they want to abolish Norfolk County government, which oversees the Norfolk County Agricultural High School and owns courthouses. Six county goverenments still exist across the state, and the Dedham man who got the measure on the ballot says they're outdated. | CBS Boston
